skills-frq-s1.title: A practice part and one student's answer (written for practice, LevlPrep 2026)
skills-frq-s1.text:
Part C (1 point). Explain one reason why many people in rural Country A move to its capital city.

Student answer: "Jobs."

skills-frq-s2.title: A second practice part and answer (written for practice, LevlPrep 2026)
skills-frq-s2.text:
Part G (1 point). Explain the degree to which data for each province of Country A are more useful than one national figure for deciding where to build new clinics.

Student answer: "Province data show which provinces have the fewest clinics, so the government can build where the need is greatest."

items.q: Would this answer earn the point for Part C?
options: No: it names a reason but does not say how jobs in the capital lead people to move
Yes: "jobs" is a correct reason, and a correct reason earns the point whatever the verb asks
No: the answer needs a number from a data source
Yes: short answers are scored higher because they are clear

why.correct: An explain answer needs a cause, a link word (because, so) and an effect tied to the place asked about.
options: Right: "explain" asks for the how or why. "Jobs" names a factor; the link to moving is missing.
A correct name earns an identify point. An explain needs the link: why jobs make people move.
This part has no stimulus and asks for no number; it asks for a reason with its link.
Readers score what the verb demands, not the length. Here the verb demands a link that is missing.

items.q: Which rewrite of the student's answer would earn the point?
options: "Jobs are a very important reason why people move to the capital city of Country A."
"The capital has more paid jobs than rural areas, so people move there to earn higher wages."
"There are jobs in the capital city of Country A, and there are also schools and hospitals there."
"Rural people in Country A move to the capital city, which is a large and busy city."

why.correct: A full explain answer has every link: more paid jobs in the capital, so people move there to earn higher wages.
options: This says jobs matter but never says how they cause people to move.
Right: it gives the cause (more paid jobs), the link (so) and the effect (people move to earn more).
This lists more factors but links none of them to moving.
This restates the question and adds a description; restating earns nothing.

items.q: Which task verb would the student's one-word answer, "Jobs", fully satisfy?
options: Explain
Describe
Identify
Compare

why.correct: Identify is the only verb a single word can satisfy. Every other verb asks for more.
options: Explain asks for the how or why, which a single word does not give.
Describe asks for features: what it is like, where and how much.
Right: identify asks you to name the thing; a word or phrase is enough.
Compare asks about two things and needs both sides.

items.q: What does this answer still need to earn the point?
options: A second province named, to give the answer more places
A definition of a clinic, so the reader knows the term
A comparison with another country that has more clinics
A stated degree at the start, such as "To a high degree"

why.correct: For "explain the degree", open with the degree (high, moderate or low), then give the reasoning.
options: Naming more places can help, but the missing piece is the degree the verb asks for.
The part does not ask for a definition.
No other country is part of the question.
Right: "explain the degree" asks you to state a degree first, then explain it. The explanation here is good; the degree is missing.

items.q: The answer says province data are more useful. At what scale of analysis are province data?
options: Local (subnational)
National (one value for the country)
Regional (a group of countries)
Global (the whole world)

why.correct: Data for parts of a country are at the local (subnational) scale, even when the map shows the whole country.
options: Right: each value is for a province, a part of the country.
National data would give one value for the whole of Country A.
The regional scale is a group of countries.
The global scale compares places across the world.

items.q: Which opening would make the answer fully match its verb?
options: "Province data are data for each province, which is part of a country..."
"To a high degree: province data show which provinces have the fewest clinics, so..."
"Clinics are places where people get health care, such as doctors..."
"National data and province data are two kinds of data that..."

why.correct: State the degree, then the because or so: "To a high degree: ... so ...".
options: A definition of province data does not state a degree or explain it.
Right: it states the degree first and keeps the reasoning with its "so".
Defining a clinic answers a different verb, define, about a different term.
This starts a comparison without stating a degree.

items.q: Which task verb asks you to speak about both of two things?
options: Describe
Identify
Compare
Define

why.correct: Compare needs both sides: "A is ..., whereas B is ...".
options: Describe gives the features of one thing or pattern.
Identify names one thing.
Right: a compare answer says how two things are alike or different, and speaks of both.
Define gives the meaning of one term.

items.q: A part asks: "Describe the pattern of farming shown on the map." Which answer earns the point?
options: "The farms are spread out in some places and close together in others on this map."
"Farming is important to Country A because many people there work on farms and sell crops in nearby towns."
"Farms are found in Country A, as the map shows."
"Most farms are along the river in the south of Country A, and few are in the dry hills of the north."

why.correct: A describe answer for a pattern says where, what and how much, with named places.
options: This names no place, so it does not describe a pattern a reader can check.
This gives a reason (an explain) instead of the pattern (a describe), and names no place.
This says farms exist but gives no where, what or how much, so it does not describe a pattern.
Right: it says where (along the river, in the south), what (most farms) and the contrast with the north.

items.q: Build an explain answer that would earn a point: why might a new highway change where people in a city shop?

specific.model: In Country A's capital, the new highway cuts the driving time to stores on the edge of the city, so more people shop there instead of downtown.

place.label: Place
options: Country A's capital
some cities

why.1: Too vague: name the place the answer is about.

cause.label: Cause
options: cuts the driving time to stores on the edge of the city
is a large road

why.1: That describes the highway but gives no cause that would change shopping.

effect.label: Effect
options: more people shop there instead of downtown
the highway is busy

why.1: That is not about where people shop, which is what the question asks.

why.correct: Place, cause, link word, effect: each link of the chain is written out.

items.q: Each free-response question on the AP® Human Geography exam has parts A to G. How are the parts scored?
options: Each part is worth 1 point, judged against one rubric line
Each part is worth up to 3 points for longer answers
The whole question is scored once, for overall quality
Points go to answers that use the most key terms

why.correct: Seven one-point parts, each checked against one rubric line: do exactly what each verb asks.
options: Right: seven parts, one point each, so each question is worth 7 points.
Writing more does not earn more points; each part has one point.
Readers score part by part, so a strong Part A cannot make up for a missing Part B.
Terms help only when they do what the verb asks; listing terms earns nothing.
